_note: Receptor targets per drug, for the what-if viewer only. This is not a dosing reference and not a treatment recommendation. Doses are shown for recognition and never reach the model.
_affinity: 0 to 1, how strongly the drug acts at that target relative to its own main action. Not a Ki and not comparable between drugs: it is a weight on where in the brain the effect lands, taken from the direction and relative prominence of each action in the pharmacology, and it is a judgement call.
_direction: +1 raises signalling through that target, -1 lowers it. A transporter blocker raises synaptic transmitter, so its direction is +1 even though it blocks the protein the map shows.
_proxy: True when the map is the nearest available picture of where the drug acts, not the drug's own target.

drugs.name: sertraline

targets.why: blocks the serotonin transporter, raising synaptic serotonin where terminals are densest
weak dopamine transporter activity at higher doses

drugs.note: Used in post-concussive depression and in headache. Onset over weeks, which this model does not represent at all: it shows where the effect lands, not when.

drugs.name: amitriptyline
drugs.note: Low dose amitriptyline is common for post-traumatic headache. Its antihistamine and antimuscarinic actions, which are most of why it is sedating, have no map here and are not represented.

drugs.name: nortriptyline

targets.why: noradrenaline reuptake inhibition, its main action

drugs.note: More noradrenergic and less sedating than amitriptyline.

drugs.name: methylphenidate
drugs.note: Used for post-traumatic attention and fatigue. The striatum, where most of the DAT signal sits, is outside this cortical parcellation, so what is shown is the cortical part of the effect only.

drugs.name: amantadine

targets.why: increases dopamine release and reduces reuptake

drugs.note: The best studied drug in disorders of consciousness after severe TBI. The evidence in mild TBI is much thinner.

drugs.name: propranolol

targets.why: no beta-adrenoceptor map exists in this atlas set. The noradrenaline transporter map shows where noradrenergic terminals are, which is the nearest available picture of where a central beta blockade would be felt. It is a proxy and the effect shown is a guess about location, not about size.

drugs.note: Used for post-traumatic headache prophylaxis. Shown against a proxy map, so treat the location of the effect as indicative and the magnitude as uninformative.

drugs.name: levetiracetam

targets.why: binds synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A, reducing vesicular release

drugs.note: SV2A is close to a synaptic density marker, so this map is as much about where synapses are as about where the drug acts.

drugs.name: ondansetron
drugs.why_not: 5-HT3 is its target and there is no 5-HT3 map in this atlas set. Its antiemetic action is also largely at the area postrema and in the gut, neither of which is in a cortical parcellation.

drugs.name: gabapentin
drugs.why_not: Its target is the alpha-2-delta subunit of the voltage gated calcium channel. There is no PET map of it.

drugs.name: melatonin
drugs.why_not: MT1 and MT2 have no map here, and the effect that matters is on the timing of sleep, which this model has no representation of at all.

drugs.name: acetaminophen
drugs.why_not: Its mechanism is still argued over and none of the candidates has a receptor map. Shown here because it is on most of these charts, and the honest answer is that this model has nothing to say about it.

drugs.name: ibuprofen
drugs.why_not: Cyclooxygenase inhibition, which is not a receptor with a distribution map.

drugs.name: topiramate

targets.why: positive modulation at a non-benzodiazepine site of GABA-A
it antagonises AMPA and kainate receptors, which have no map here. The mGluR5 map stands in for excitatory glutamatergic density and is a proxy.

drugs.note: Used for headache prophylaxis. Cognitive side effects are the usual reason it is stopped, and this model does not represent those.
